text: A pod named `api-server` is repeatedly restarting. Running `kubectl get pods` shows the STATUS column as `CrashLoopBackOff` with RESTARTS at 14. What does this status indicate?
options: The container image cannot be pulled from the registry
The node running the pod has run out of disk space and is evicting pods
The container starts, crashes, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with exponential back-off delays
The pod's readiness probe is failing and the pod is being removed from Service endpoints

text: You deploy a pod and it remains in the `Pending` state for over 10 minutes. Running `kubectl describe pod` shows the event: `0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The pod's CPU request exceeds the allocatable CPU on all nodes in the cluster
A `NetworkPolicy` is blocking the pod from communicating with the API server
The container image specified in the pod manifest does not exist
The pod has a `nodeSelector` that does not match any node labels

text: After deploying a new version of your application, `kubectl get pods` shows one pod with STATUS `ImagePullBackOff`. The `Events` section of `kubectl describe pod` shows `Failed to pull image "myapp:v2.1": rpc error: code = NotFound`. Which action would most directly resolve this?
options: Restart the kubelet on the node where the pod is scheduled
Delete the pod's `ServiceAccount` and recreate it
Increase the pod's memory limits to allow the image to be pulled
Verify that the image `myapp:v2.1` exists in the container registry and the tag is correct

text: A pod's container is being `OOMKilled` repeatedly. The `kubectl describe pod` output shows `Last State: Terminated` with `Reason: OOMKilled` and `Exit Code: 137`. What does this tell you about the container?
options: The container's liveness probe timed out and Kubernetes killed the process
The node ran out of disk space causing the container to be evicted
The container process consumed more memory than its configured `limits.memory` and the Linux kernel killed it
The container failed its startup probe and was terminated by the kubelet

text: Users report intermittent 503 errors when accessing your service. Some pods behind the Service are in `Running` state but their `READY` column shows `0/1`. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The pods have no resource limits configured and are being throttled
The pods are running on nodes that have been cordoned
DNS resolution for the Service name is intermittently failing
The readiness probe is failing on those pods, so they are removed from the Service's endpoint list

text: Your team is adopting a cloud native troubleshooting strategy. A microservice pod keeps crashing, but the application does not write meaningful logs to stdout. According to cloud native best practices, what should the team prioritize?
options: Refactor the application to emit structured logs to stdout/stderr so that `kubectl logs` and log aggregators can capture them
SSH into the node and read the application log files directly from the container's filesystem layer
Mount a persistent volume to store log files and set up a cron job to collect them
Disable container restarts so the crashed container's filesystem persists for analysis

text: After a node reboot, several pods are stuck in `Terminating` state and will not delete. Running `kubectl delete pod <name>` hangs indefinitely. What is the recommended approach to forcefully remove these pods?
options: `kubectl delete pod <name> --grace-period=0 --force`
`kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets`
`kubectl cordon <node-name>` followed by `kubectl uncordon <node-name>`
`kubectl rollout restart deployment <deployment-name>`

text: A multi-container pod has two containers: `app` and `sidecar-logger`. You want to view only the logs from the `app` container. Which command is correct?
options: `kubectl logs <pod-name>`
`kubectl describe pod <pod-name> | grep logs`
`kubectl logs <pod-name> -c app`
`kubectl exec <pod-name> -- cat /var/log/app.log`

text: A deployment's pods fail to start with the event: `Warning FailedScheduling: 0/5 nodes are available: 5 node(s) had taint {node.kubernetes.io/not-ready: }, that the pod didn't tolerate`. What does this mean?
options: The pod's image pull secret is missing and all nodes are refusing the pull request
The pod's `nodeAffinity` rules exclude all available nodes
The cluster's admission controller is blocking pod creation due to a security policy
All five nodes in the cluster are in a `NotReady` state, and the pods do not have a toleration for the `not-ready` taint

text: A pod has an init container that must complete before the main application container starts. The pod is stuck in `Init:CrashLoopBackOff`. What does this status mean?
options: The main application container is crashing, and the init container is trying to restart it
The init container keeps crashing and restarting, preventing the main container from ever starting
The init container completed successfully but the main container cannot find the files it created
The pod was evicted due to resource pressure and is being rescheduled

text: In a microservices architecture, Service A depends on Service B. After deploying a new version of Service B, Service A starts returning timeout errors. The pods for Service B are `Running` and `Ready`. What should you check first?
options: Whether Service B's container image was built with the correct base image
Whether the Kubernetes scheduler moved Service B pods to a different namespace
Whether Service A's pod security policy was modified during the deployment
Whether Service B's new version changed its API contract or response time, causing Service A's requests to exceed its timeout threshold

text:
You run `kubectl describe pod web-app` and see the following under Conditions:

```
Conditions:
  Type     Status
  PodScheduled   True
  Initialized    True
  ContainersReady False
  Ready          False
```

What can you conclude?
options: The pod has not yet been assigned to a node by the scheduler
The pod's init containers have not completed yet
The pod is scheduled and init containers finished, but at least one main container is not passing its readiness check
The pod's volumes have failed to mount and all containers are waiting

text: A pod fails to start with the event: `Error: container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root`. What must you change to fix this?
options: Remove the `readinessProbe` from the pod spec since it conflicts with the security context
Add a `ClusterRoleBinding` that grants the pod's ServiceAccount root access
Ensure the container image runs as a non-root user, or set `runAsUser` to a non-zero UID in the pod's `securityContext`
Set `privileged: true` in the container's security context to bypass the restriction

text: After a rolling update, some pods from the new ReplicaSet are in `CrashLoopBackOff` while old pods were terminated. Users are experiencing downtime. What deployment setting could have prevented this scenario?
options: Configuring `minReadySeconds` and a proper readiness probe so the deployment waits for new pods to become healthy before terminating old ones
Setting `spec.strategy.type` to `Recreate` to replace all pods simultaneously
Increasing the `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to give the old pods more time to shut down
Adding a `PodDisruptionBudget` with `maxUnavailable: 100%`

text: A pod is stuck in `Pending` state. The events show: `0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had taint {gpu=true: NoSchedule}, 2 node(s) had taint {maintenance: NoSchedule}`. The pod needs to run on the GPU node. What should you add to the pod spec?
options: A `nodeSelector` matching the GPU node's labels
A toleration for the taint `gpu=true:NoSchedule`
An annotation `scheduler.alpha.kubernetes.io/gpu-required: "true"`
A resource request for `nvidia.com/gpu: 1`

text: A pod can reach other pods by IP address but DNS lookups for Service names fail. Running `kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup kubernetes.default` returns `connection timed out; no servers could be reached`. Which component should you investigate?
options: The `kube-scheduler`, as it may have placed the pod on an isolated node
The `kube-proxy` DaemonSet, which manages iptables rules for Services
The CoreDNS pods in the `kube-system` namespace, which provide cluster DNS resolution
The `etcd` cluster, which stores all DNS records for the cluster

text: You want to watch pod restarts in real-time across all namespaces to identify unstable workloads. Which command provides a continuously updating view?
options: `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --sort-by='.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount'`
`kubectl get pods -A --watch`
`kubectl top pods --all-namespaces`
`kubectl get events --all-namespaces --field-selector reason=Killing`

text: A container's liveness probe is configured as an HTTP GET to `/healthz` on port 8080. The application takes 30 seconds to initialize, but the probe starts checking at container start with `initialDelaySeconds: 5`. What will happen?
options: The pod will enter `ImagePullBackOff` because the health endpoint is not responsive
The container will be marked as not ready but will continue running until it passes the probe
The liveness probe will automatically wait for the readiness probe to pass first
The kubelet will kill and restart the container because the liveness probe fails during initialization, creating a `CrashLoopBackOff` cycle

text: Your team needs to debug a production container that was built from a minimal/distroless image with no shell or debugging tools. Which Kubernetes feature allows you to attach a debugging container to the running pod?
options: `kubectl debug <pod-name> --image=busybox --target=<container-name>` to create an ephemeral debug container
`kubectl cp` to copy a debug binary into the running container
`kubectl exec <pod-name> -- /bin/sh` to start a shell in the existing container
`kubectl replace --force` to redeploy the pod with a different image

text:
A Deployment with 3 replicas shows the following after `kubectl get pods`:

```
NAME                   READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
web-6d8f9b-abc12       1/1     Running            0          2d
web-6d8f9b-def34       1/1     Running            0          2d
web-7c4e2a-ghi56       0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   8          12m
```

What can you infer about the deployment?
options: All three pods are from the same ReplicaSet and one has a corrupted container filesystem
A rolling update created a new ReplicaSet (`7c4e2a`), but the new pod is crashing, while two old pods (`6d8f9b`) remain healthy
The third pod was manually created outside of the Deployment and is unrelated
The Deployment's replica count was reduced from 3 to 2 and the excess pod is being terminated

text: A pod is stuck in `Pending` with the event: `persistentvolumeclaim "data-pvc" not found`. The PVC exists in the cluster but the pod remains unscheduled. What is the most likely cause?
options: The PVC and the pod are in different namespaces
The PVC's storage class does not support dynamic provisioning
The PVC is in `Bound` state and cannot be used by another pod
The node where the pod would be scheduled does not have enough disk space

text: Your CI/CD pipeline deploys a new image tag but the pods still run the old version. The Deployment spec uses `image: myapp:latest` and `imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent`. What explains this behavior?
options: The Kubernetes API server cached the old image tag and needs to be restarted
The deployment controller does not detect tag changes when the image name stays the same
The container runtime does not support pulling images with the `latest` tag
Since `imagePullPolicy` is `IfNotPresent`, the node uses the already-cached `myapp:latest` image instead of pulling the updated version

text: A team discovers that a failing pod emits zero logs via `kubectl logs`, making debugging impossible. Investigating the container reveals the application writes logs to `/var/log/app.log` inside the container. Which pattern would improve observability without modifying the application code?
options: Deploy a sidecar container that tails `/var/log/app.log` to its own stdout, making the logs available via `kubectl logs -c <sidecar>`
Mount a `hostPath` volume so the log file is written directly to the node's filesystem for collection
Configure the kubelet to automatically detect log files inside containers and forward them
Set the pod's `restartPolicy` to `Never` so the container's filesystem is preserved after failure

text: After upgrading the cluster, `kubectl get nodes` shows one node as `NotReady`. Running `kubectl describe node` shows the condition `KubeletNotReady` with message `runtime network not ready: NetworkReady=false`. What component is likely misconfigured?
options: The `kube-apiserver`, which cannot communicate with the node's kubelet
The `kube-scheduler`, which failed to register the node after the upgrade
The CNI plugin on the node, which provides pod networking and reports readiness to the kubelet
The `etcd` instance on that node, which stores the node's network configuration

text: You run `kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'` and see repeated `BackOff` events for a pod. The event message says `Back-off restarting failed container`. What information should you check next to determine why the container is failing?
options: The pod's `metadata.annotations` for error codes injected by the scheduler
The container's exit code and logs from the previous run using `kubectl logs <pod> --previous`
The node's kubelet certificate expiry date
The pod's `ownerReferences` field to identify the parent controller

text: A StatefulSet pod `db-0` is in `CrashLoopBackOff`. You discover the application fails because it cannot write to `/data`. Running `kubectl exec db-0 -- ls -la /data` shows the directory is owned by `root` but the container runs as UID `1000`. What is the fix?
options: Delete the PersistentVolumeClaim and let the StatefulSet recreate it with correct permissions
Change the StatefulSet's `replicas` to 0 and back to 1 to trigger a fresh volume mount
Set `imagePullPolicy: Always` to force a fresh image pull with correct file permissions
Add an `initContainer` that runs as root and executes `chown 1000:1000 /data` before the main container starts

text: A Service of type `ClusterIP` is created for a Deployment, but `curl <service-ip>:<port>` from within the cluster returns `connection refused`. The pods are `Running` and `Ready`. What should you verify?
options: That the Service's `spec.selector` labels match the pod labels, and the `targetPort` matches the port the application listens on
That a `NetworkPolicy` with an explicit `allow` rule for the Service IP exists
That the `kube-apiserver` has the `--enable-aggregator-routing` flag enabled
That the pods have a `ClusterIP` annotation in their metadata

text: A pod shows `STATUS: Error` and `Exit Code: 1` after running to completion. The pod's `restartPolicy` is `Never`. What will Kubernetes do with this pod?
options: Kubernetes will automatically restart the pod after an exponential back-off delay
The pod will remain in `Error` state indefinitely because `restartPolicy: Never` prevents restarts
Kubernetes will delete the failed pod and schedule a replacement on a different node
The pod will transition to `Pending` state and wait for manual intervention

text: A pod remains `Pending` with the event: `0/4 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient memory, 2 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector`. How many distinct issues prevent scheduling?
options: Two distinct issues: two nodes lack memory capacity, and two other nodes do not match the pod's affinity or selector rules
One issue: all nodes have insufficient memory because node affinity overrides memory checks
Three issues: memory, affinity, and an implicit CPU shortage on all nodes
One issue: the node selector is misconfigured which causes the scheduler to misreport memory availability

text: A pod fails with the event: `Failed to create pod sandbox: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to start sandbox container: Error response from daemon: OCI runtime create failed`. Which layer of the container stack is reporting this error?
options: The kube-scheduler, which could not find a valid node for the pod
The kube-apiserver, which rejected the pod spec during admission
The CNI plugin, which failed to assign a network namespace to the pod
The CRI implementation (e.g., containerd) relaying an error from the low-level OCI runtime (e.g., `runc`)

text: A 12-factor application running in Kubernetes fails because an environment variable `DATABASE_URL` is empty. The pod spec references a ConfigMap that exists but does not contain the key `DATABASE_URL`. What is the pod's expected behavior?
options: The pod starts normally but the environment variable is set to an empty string, causing application errors at runtime
The pod fails immediately with a `CreateContainerConfigError` status because the referenced key does not exist in the ConfigMap
The pod starts but Kubernetes automatically injects a default value of `localhost` for missing ConfigMap keys
The pod enters `Pending` state while the scheduler waits for the ConfigMap to be updated

text: You notice a pod with `STATUS: Completed` and `RESTARTS: 0` in `kubectl get pods`. The pod belongs to a Job resource. Is this pod healthy?
options: No, `Completed` means the pod crashed after finishing its work
No, the pod should show `Running` if the Job succeeded
Yes, `Completed` with exit code 0 means the Job's container ran successfully and exited normally
Yes, but only if the Job's `backoffLimit` has not been reached

text: You want to identify which pods are consuming the most CPU and memory in a namespace. Which command provides real-time resource usage metrics?
options: `kubectl describe pods -n <namespace>` and look for resource fields
`kubectl get pods -n <namespace> -o wide` with the `--show-metrics` flag
`kubectl top pods -n <namespace> --sort-by=cpu`
`kubectl get resourcequota -n <namespace>` to see per-pod consumption

text: A pod running a web server is accessible from within the cluster but not from external traffic through a `NodePort` Service. The Service is correctly configured with `type: NodePort` and `nodePort: 30080`. What should you check on the nodes?
options: Whether the pod has an explicit `externalTrafficPolicy` annotation set to `Local`
Whether the pod's container has the `NET_ADMIN` capability in its security context
Whether the pod's `hostNetwork` field is set to `true`
Whether the node's firewall or security group allows inbound traffic on port 30080

text: A DaemonSet pod on a specific node keeps getting `OOMKilled`. Other DaemonSet pods on different nodes are running fine. The pod's memory limit is 256Mi. What should you investigate on that specific node?
options: Whether the node has more workloads competing for memory, causing the DaemonSet pod's application to hit its limit faster due to system memory pressure
Whether the DaemonSet's update strategy is `OnDelete` instead of `RollingUpdate`
Whether the node has a different container runtime than other nodes
Whether the `kube-proxy` on that node is consuming excessive memory

text: A `startupProbe` is configured on a container with `failureThreshold: 30` and `periodSeconds: 10`. The application takes about 3 minutes to initialize. What is the purpose of the `startupProbe` in this scenario?
options: It replaces the readiness probe entirely and determines when the pod receives traffic
It continuously monitors the application and restarts it if startup takes longer than 30 seconds
It gives the application up to 300 seconds to start before the liveness and readiness probes begin their checks
It signals the scheduler to delay placing additional pods until this one is healthy

text: A pod fails to pull an image from a private container registry. The event shows: `Failed to pull image: unauthorized: authentication required`. The correct `imagePullSecrets` was created but the pod still cannot authenticate. What is a common mistake?
options: The Secret was created with `type: Opaque` instead of `type: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`
The node's kubelet is configured to ignore image pull secrets for security reasons
The container image tag is set to `latest` which bypasses authentication
The Secret's data must be base64-encoded twice for Docker registry authentication

text: In a distributed microservices system, a chain of calls (A -> B -> C) is experiencing intermittent failures. Service C's pods are healthy, but Service B logs show `context deadline exceeded` when calling Service C. What technique would help pinpoint the latency source?
options: Increasing the replica count of Service C to handle more requests
Restarting all pods in the chain to clear any stale connections
Implementing distributed tracing (e.g., Jaeger or Zipkin) to visualize latency across each hop in the request chain
Adding CPU resource limits to all services to prevent noisy-neighbor problems

text: After running `helm upgrade myrelease ./mychart`, several pods are in `CrashLoopBackOff`. You need to quickly restore the previous working version. Which Helm command achieves this?
options: `helm rollback myrelease`
`helm uninstall myrelease` and then `helm install myrelease ./mychart`
`helm template myrelease ./mychart | kubectl delete -f -`
`helm repo update && helm upgrade myrelease --reset-values ./mychart`

text: Running `kubectl` commands from your workstation returns: `Unable to connect to the server: dial tcp <ip>:6443: connect: connection refused`. The cluster was working an hour ago. What should you check first?
options: Whether the `kube-apiserver` process is running on the control plane node
Whether the `etcd` data directory has been encrypted
Whether a new RBAC policy is blocking your user account
Whether the cluster's Ingress controller is healthy

text: A pod can resolve DNS names for Services in its own namespace using short names (e.g., `my-service`) but fails to resolve Services in other namespaces. What is the correct DNS format to reach a Service in a different namespace?
options: `<service-name>.<namespace>`
`<namespace>/<service-name>`
`<service-name>--<namespace>.cluster.local`
`<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`

text: A pod enters `CrashLoopBackOff` immediately after starting. The `kubectl logs` output is empty, and `kubectl logs --previous` also returns nothing. What does the absence of logs suggest?
options: The application is writing logs to stderr instead of stdout, which `kubectl logs` does not capture
The pod's log rotation policy deleted the logs before you could view them
The container process crashes before producing any output, likely during the entrypoint or command execution phase
The kubelet on the node has logging disabled via a configuration flag

text: A pod has `restartPolicy: Always` and its single container exits with code 0. What does Kubernetes do?
options: The pod transitions to `Completed` state and is never restarted
Kubernetes restarts the container because `restartPolicy: Always` means it restarts regardless of the exit code
The pod is deleted and a new pod is created by the ReplicaSet controller
The kubelet marks the pod as `Failed` because containers should not exit with code 0 under this policy

text: You need to retrieve logs from a pod that crashed and was replaced 2 hours ago. The new pod has the same name. `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` shows logs from the current pod's previous restart, not from the pod that was replaced. How can you retrieve the old logs?
options: The old pod's logs are permanently lost unless a cluster-level log aggregation system (e.g., Fluentd, Loki) was collecting them
Use `kubectl logs <pod> --since=3h` to reach back in time to the old pod's logs
Run `kubectl describe pod <pod>` which stores the last 1000 log lines from all previous pod instances
Use `kubectl get events` which automatically captures full container logs on termination

text: Your team uses Prometheus to monitor Kubernetes workloads. A pod's memory usage steadily climbs until it gets `OOMKilled`, then restarts and repeats the pattern. What Prometheus metric would help you detect this memory leak before the OOM event?
options: `kube_pod_status_phase` filtered to `Failed`
`kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total` to count restarts
`node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes` to monitor overall node memory
`container_memory_working_set_bytes` tracked over time, showing a continuous upward trend approaching the memory limit

text: A pod with two containers shows `READY: 1/2`. One container is in `Waiting` state with reason `CrashLoopBackOff`. Can the healthy container continue to serve traffic through a Service?
options: Yes, Services route traffic to individual containers, so the healthy one still receives requests
No, the pod is removed from the Service's Endpoints because the overall pod readiness is `False` when any container is not ready
Yes, but only if the Service uses `sessionAffinity: ClientIP`
No, Kubernetes immediately terminates the entire pod when any container crashes

text: You apply a ConfigMap change and restart the pods, but the application still reads old configuration values. The ConfigMap is mounted as a volume (not as environment variables). What could explain this?
options: ConfigMap volume mounts are immutable after pod creation and require a pod delete/recreate
ConfigMap changes are only propagated by the kubelet every 24 hours
The application caches the configuration file at startup and does not re-read it from disk, so a restart should have loaded the new values—verify the pod actually restarted
The `kube-controller-manager` must be restarted for ConfigMap changes to propagate

text: A GitOps tool (e.g., ArgoCD) shows a Deployment as `OutOfSync` after someone manually ran `kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5` in the cluster. The Git repository defines `replicas: 3`. What will happen on the next sync?
options: ArgoCD will revert the Deployment to `replicas: 3` to match the desired state in Git
ArgoCD will preserve the manual change and update the Git repository to `replicas: 5`
ArgoCD will average the values and set `replicas: 4`
ArgoCD will mark the Deployment as failed and stop syncing until manually resolved

text: A CronJob runs every hour but you notice some Jobs are missing from the expected schedule. The CronJob's `concurrencyPolicy` is set to `Forbid`. What does this policy cause?
options: It prevents the CronJob from running entirely if any other Job in the namespace is active
It terminates the currently running Job to start the new scheduled one
It queues the new Job and runs it immediately after the current one finishes
It skips a new Job run if the previous Job from this CronJob has not yet completed

text: You run `kubectl describe pod payment-svc` and see a `Warning` event: `Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503`. The pod is `Running` but `READY: 0/1`. What is the operational impact?
options: The pod will be killed and restarted by the kubelet after the failure threshold is met
The pod continues running but is excluded from the Service's Endpoints, so it receives no traffic
The pod will be evicted from the node and rescheduled on a healthier node
There is no impact because readiness probes are informational only

text: A pod with `resources.requests.memory: 8Gi` is `Pending` in a cluster where the largest node has 16Gi total memory but only 6Gi allocatable. What does 'allocatable' mean in this context?
options: The total physical RAM installed on the node, minus memory used by running pods
The memory limit specified in the node's LimitRange resource
The maximum memory that a single pod can request according to the ResourceQuota
The memory available for pod scheduling after reserving memory for the kubelet, system daemons, and OS overhead

text: After scaling a Deployment from 3 to 10 replicas, 7 new pods stay in `Pending`. The events show `0/5 nodes are available: 5 Insufficient cpu`. The existing 3 pods use `requests.cpu: 500m` each. What is the most effective resolution?
options: Increase the `limits.cpu` on the existing pods to give them more processing power
Change the Deployment strategy from `RollingUpdate` to `Recreate`
Either reduce the CPU requests per pod, add nodes with more CPU capacity, or use the cluster autoscaler to provision new nodes
Set `priorityClassName: system-node-critical` on the Deployment to preempt existing workloads

text: A container's readiness probe is configured as a TCP socket check on port 5432. The application (PostgreSQL) takes 15 seconds to start accepting connections. During those 15 seconds, what is the readiness probe result?
options: The TCP check succeeds immediately because the kernel binds the port as soon as the container starts
The TCP check fails because no process is listening on port 5432 yet, and the pod is marked as not ready
The TCP check is skipped until the liveness probe passes first
The TCP check times out and the container is killed by the kubelet

text: After deploying a `NetworkPolicy` that selects pods with label `app=api`, those pods can no longer communicate with any other pods. The NetworkPolicy only has an `ingress` rule allowing traffic from `app=frontend`. What caused the complete communication breakdown?
options: Once any NetworkPolicy selects a pod, all ingress not explicitly allowed is denied by default; if `policyTypes` also includes `Egress`, outbound traffic is denied too unless explicitly allowed
The NetworkPolicy blocks all traffic including DNS, so the pods cannot resolve any hostnames
NetworkPolicies require a corresponding `allow-all` egress rule to be created in a separate resource
The CNI plugin does not support NetworkPolicy enforcement on this cluster

text: A Deployment's rollout is stuck. Running `kubectl rollout status deployment/app` shows `Waiting for deployment "app" rollout to finish: 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...`. The single new pod is in `CrashLoopBackOff`. What parameter controls how long Kubernetes waits before marking the rollout as failed?
options: `spec.template.spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds`
`spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge`
`spec.minReadySeconds`
`spec.progressDeadlineSeconds`

text: A team is debugging an application that works locally in Docker but fails in Kubernetes with `exec format error`. The cluster nodes run on `linux/amd64`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The container image was built for a different CPU architecture (e.g., `linux/arm64`) and cannot run on `amd64` nodes
The Kubernetes version is incompatible with the Docker version used to build the image
The container runtime does not support the OCI image format
The pod's security context prevents execution of the container's entrypoint binary

text: A pod in a StatefulSet named `cache-2` fails and is recreated. Unlike Deployments, the new pod has the exact same name `cache-2`. Why does this matter for troubleshooting?
options: It does not matter because pod names are only cosmetic identifiers
It causes DNS conflicts because two pods with the same name temporarily exist during replacement
The stable identity means the pod reattaches to the same PersistentVolumeClaim and DNS hostname, so persistent data and network identity are preserved across restarts
The kubelet refuses to create a pod with a name that was previously used, causing the StatefulSet to stall

text: You see this event in `kubectl describe pod`: `Warning  Unhealthy  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.1.5:8080/healthz": dial tcp 10.244.1.5:8080: connect: connection refused`. The container was previously running fine. What should you check?
options: Whether the application inside the container has crashed or stopped listening on port 8080
Whether the CNI plugin has revoked the pod's IP address
Whether the Kubernetes API server can reach the pod's IP address directly
Whether the liveness probe URL path `/healthz` was renamed in the pod spec

text: A microservice mesh experiences cascading failures: when Service D becomes slow, Services C, B, and A all start timing out. What design pattern should be implemented to prevent this cascade?
options: Increasing the timeout values in all upstream services to wait longer for Service D
Adding more replicas to Service D to handle the increased load
Deploying all four services in the same pod to eliminate network latency
Implementing the circuit breaker pattern so that upstream services fail fast when Service D is unhealthy instead of waiting for timeouts

text: A node reports `DiskPressure: True` in its conditions. Pods on this node start getting evicted with `The node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage`. What type of storage is being exhausted?
options: The PersistentVolumes attached to the pods on that node
The etcd data directory on the control plane node
